source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Religious Studies past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: At the end of Ramadan, Muslim families in Douala, Garoua, Foumban and other towns put on new clothes, gather for the special morning prayer and visit relatives. About two months later, at the time of the pilgrimage to Makkah, many families sacrifice an animal and share its meat. These two celebrations are the festivals most often set in Religious Studies papers. In both Paper 1 and Paper 2 you may be asked to state the name or date of a festival, to explain why it is celebrated or to judge whether it is mainly religious or social. This lesson gives you the facts and a method for each type of question.

items: The five pillars of Islam are Shahada, Salat, Zakat, Sawm and Hajj.
Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar, during which adult Muslims fast from dawn to sunset.
Muslims regard Ibrahim (Abraham) as a prophet of God, and the Hajj is the pilgrimage to Makkah in the last month of the Islamic year.

sections.titre: The festivals of Islam: the two Eids and other observances
sections.contenu_markdown:
### The two main festivals
'Eid' (also written Id) is the Arabic word for a festival. The two Eids are celebrated by Muslims all over the world.

| | Eid al-Fitr (Id-ul-Fitr) | Eid al-Adha (Id-ul-Adha) |
|---|---|---|
| Date | First day of Shawwal, the tenth month, immediately after Ramadan | Tenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, the twelfth month, during the Hajj |
| Meaning | Marks the end of the fast of Ramadan; Muslims give thanks to God for the strength to fast | Commemorates the obedience of Ibrahim, who was ready to sacrifice his son at God's command, and the animal that God provided in the son's place |
| Practices | Special congregational prayer in the morning; Zakat al-Fitr (a charitable gift for the poor, traditionally of food) given before the prayer; new or best clothes, visits, gifts and shared meals; fasting is not permitted on this day | Special congregational prayer in the morning; sacrifice of an animal such as a sheep, goat, cow or camel by those who can afford it; the meat is shared with family, neighbours and the poor |
| Link | Closes the month of fasting | Falls during the Hajj, the day after the pilgrims stand at Arafat, so pilgrims and Muslims at home celebrate on the same day |

Islamic tradition commonly names the son as Ismail. Muslims understand the sacrifice as an act of obedience, gratitude and sharing, not as a gift of meat to God.

### The Islamic calendar
It has twelve lunar months of about 354 days, and months begin with the sighting of the new moon. Festivals therefore move earlier by about ten or eleven days each year in the solar calendar, and the date can differ by a day from one place to another.

### Other observances
- **Mawlid al-Nabi**: remembrance of the birth of the Prophet Muhammad, marked on 12 Rabi al-Awwal by many Muslims, while some Muslims do not observe it.
- **Islamic New Year (1 Muharram)**: marks the Hijra, the migration of Muhammad and his followers from Makkah to Madinah, from which the calendar counts.
- **Ashura (10 Muharram)**: observed in different ways by Sunni and Shia Muslims.
- **Laylat al-Qadr (Night of Power)**: one of the last ten nights of Ramadan, remembering the beginning of the revelation of the Quran.

### Religious or social?
Both Eids have a religious core (prayer, charity, remembrance) and a social side (clothes, visits, meals, gifts). A balanced answer shows that the social joy expresses the religious meaning.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the reason for a festival is asked.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give the date, the event or belief it commemorates, and one or two practices that express it. For Eid al-Adha: the story of Ibrahim, the link with the Hajj and the sharing of meat.

variantes.nom: Question that asks you to evaluate a statement
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to evaluate, assess or discuss whether a festival is mainly religious or social.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Present the religious side, then the social side, then judge. Show that the two are connected, because the visits, gifts and meals are the form in which the religious ideas of thanks, charity and brotherhood are lived.

sections.enonce_markdown: Explain how the festival of Eid al-Adha links the story of Ibrahim, the Hajj and care for the poor. (12 marks)

etapes.justification: There are three links to explain, and 'explain' asks for connections, not only description.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Plan: introduction with the date; Ibrahim; the Hajj; the poor; conclusion.

etapes.justification: The date and the name give a base for the rest.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Eid al-Adha is celebrated on the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, the twelfth month, with a special congregational prayer.

etapes.justification: The reason for the festival is the core of the answer.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Muslims remember that Ibrahim was ready to sacrifice his son in obedience to God and that God provided an animal in his place; they re-enact his obedience by sacrificing an animal.

etapes.action: Explain the link with the Hajj.
etapes.justification: The timing connects the festival with the pilgrimage.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The festival falls during the Hajj, the day after the pilgrims stand at Arafat, so pilgrims and Muslims all over the world celebrate together.

etapes.action: Explain the link with the poor and conclude.
etapes.justification: Sharing the meat shows the social meaning.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The meat is divided among the family, neighbours and the poor, so the sacrifice becomes an act of charity and unity.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer (key points).** Eid al-Adha takes place on the tenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah. Muslims remember how Ibrahim was ready to obey God by sacrificing his son and how God provided an animal instead, and those who can afford it sacrifice an animal in remembrance. The festival falls during the Hajj, the day after the pilgrims stand at Arafat, which links Muslims at home with the pilgrims in Makkah in one celebration. The meat is shared with relatives, neighbours and the poor, so the festival expresses obedience to God and also care for others. It therefore joins the story of Ibrahim, the unity of the worldwide community and charity.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that Eid al-Adha marks the end of Ramadan.
items.pourquoi_faux: This confuses the two festivals. The end of Ramadan is marked by Eid al-Fitr; Eid al-Adha falls on the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah during the Hajj.
items.correction_markdown: Link Eid al-Fitr with Ramadan and Shawwal, and Eid al-Adha with the Hajj, Dhu al-Hijjah and the story of Ibrahim.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that Ibrahim sacrificed his son.
items.pourquoi_faux: According to Islamic teaching Ibrahim was ready to do so, but God provided an animal instead, and the son was not sacrificed.
items.correction_markdown: Write that Ibrahim was ready to sacrifice his son and that a substitute was provided.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving a fixed date in the solar calendar, such as a particular day in July.
items.pourquoi_faux: Islamic festivals follow the lunar calendar, so their date in the solar year changes every year.
items.correction_markdown: Give the Islamic date (1 Shawwal, 10 Dhu al-Hijjah) and explain that the solar date moves about ten or eleven days earlier each year.

items.erreur_markdown: Describing a festival only by its feasting and clothes.
items.pourquoi_faux: This ignores the religious core. Examiners expect prayer, charity and the event commemorated.
items.correction_markdown: Mention the special prayer, Zakat al-Fitr or the sacrifice, and then the social customs.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing 'Muslims sacrifice the animal to feed God'.
items.pourquoi_faux: Muslims understand the sacrifice as an act of obedience and gratitude to God, who needs nothing, and the meat is shared among people.
items.correction_markdown: Write that Muslims sacrifice in remembrance of Ibrahim's obedience and share the meat.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the two main festivals of Islam and state the Islamic month in which each falls. (4 marks)
items.solution_markdown: **Eid al-Fitr** falls in Shawwal, the tenth month, at the end of Ramadan, and **Eid al-Adha** falls in Dhu al-Hijjah, the twelfth month, at the time of the Hajj. Award 1 mark for each festival and 1 mark for each month.

items.enonce_markdown: Describe how Muslims celebrate Eid al-Fitr. (6 marks)
items.solution_markdown: Award marks for points such as: it begins after the sighting of the new moon that ends Ramadan; Zakat al-Fitr is given to the poor before the prayer; Muslims gather for the special congregational prayer, often in a large mosque or open ground; they wear new or best clothes; they greet one another with wishes such as 'Eid Mubarak'; families visit, exchange gifts and share a meal; fasting is not permitted on that day. **Six developed points, one mark each, or three points with development.**

items.enonce_markdown: To what extent do the Islamic festivals unite Muslims across the world? (15 marks)
items.solution_markdown: Plan and marking points. Introduction: the two Eids defined (2 marks). Unity: all Muslims celebrate the same festivals, with the same special prayer, greetings and charity; Eid al-Adha coincides with the Hajj; Zakat al-Fitr and the sharing of meat link rich and poor; shared meals and visits strengthen families and communities (up to 7 marks). Limits: dates may differ by a day from place to place because of moon sighting; local customs, food and clothing vary; some observances, such as Mawlid and Ashura, are kept differently or not kept by all Muslims (up to 4 marks). Conclusion: a judgement that the Eids are strong signs of unity, while local variety shows the cultures of different regions (2 marks). **Credit a balanced, supported judgement.**

items_markdown: The two main festivals are Eid al-Fitr (1 Shawwal, end of Ramadan) and Eid al-Adha (10 Dhu al-Hijjah, during the Hajj).
Eid al-Fitr: special prayer, Zakat al-Fitr before the prayer, thanks for the strength to fast, clothes, visits and meals.
Eid al-Adha: remembers Ibrahim's obedience and the animal provided in place of his son; the sacrifice is shared with family, neighbours and the poor.
The Islamic calendar is lunar, so festival dates move earlier by about ten or eleven days each year in the solar calendar.
Other observances include Mawlid, the Islamic New Year, Ashura and Laylat al-Qadr; some are kept differently by different groups.
In a religious-or-social question, show the religious core, the social customs and the link between them.
